\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Arabic, recognize the reply, and choose an appropriate response.}

Complete AR-C01-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: greet someone in Arabic, recognize the reply, and choose an appropriate response.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[salām]{\emph{salām} — say “peace” before meeting the page}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-salam}



\begin{quote}
Your first Arabic greeting is \emph{salām}. For this lesson, keep your eyes off the script. Put the sound and meaning in your ear first; the next two tiny lessons will reveal its written pieces without asking you to swallow four new shapes at once.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it in two easy beats: \emph{sa} — \emph{lām}. Hold the second \emph{a} a little longer: \emph{sa-LAAM}. The last sound is a clean \emph{m}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{salām} = peace; as a greeting, “peace to you.”
\end{quote}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{salām} sits on the three-consonant root \textbf{s–l–m}, carrying the idea of wholeness, safety, and peace. The same family gives \emph{islām}, \emph{muslim}, and \emph{sallama}, “to greet.” Hebrew \emph{shalom} is a close Semitic cousin, and English borrowed \emph{salaam}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sa} — \emph{lām}
  \item \emph{salām}, with the long vowel in the second beat
  \item “peace,” while offering \emph{salām} to an imagined person
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing — first microstep}
Only after you can say the greeting, meet one isolated shape: \textbf{\ar{س}} is \emph{sīn}, the \emph{s} at the start of \emph{salām}. Notice three small teeth and a trailing bowl. Trace \textbf{\ar{س}} once with a finger, hide it, then air-write the three teeth. Do not decode or copy the complete word yet.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{س}} once, then compare its three teeth with the model
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{salām} offer? (\textbf{Peace.}) Which three consonants carry its root? (\textbf{s–l–m.}) Which one shape did you trace? (\textbf{\ar{س}, sīn.}) Say the word once more. Do not decode or copy the complete word yet.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sīn, lām]{\ar{س} and \ar{ل} — recall one shape, add one}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-sin-lam}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{salām}. You already know what it means and traced \textbf{\ar{س}} once. Now recall that shape and add only its next consonant. Arabic runs \textbf{right to left}, so the first shape waits on the right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — recall sīn and add lām}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{س}} is \emph{sīn}, the \emph{s} sound you are retrieving from lesson one. From Phoenician \textbf{shin} (\textquotedblleft{}tooth\textquotedblright{}) — and the shape really is a row of teeth.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ل}} is \emph{lām}, the \emph{l} sound. Notice its tall upright and low curve. From Phoenician \textbf{lāmed} (\textquotedblleft{}ox-goad\textquotedblright{}) — ancestor of Greek \emph{lambda} and Latin \textbf{L}.
\end{itemize}

Slide a finger from right to left under \textbf{\ar{س} \ar{ل}} and say \emph{s — l}. Do not build the whole word yet.

\subsection*{Writing — trace, then recall}
1. Trace \textbf{\ar{س}} once with a finger: three teeth, then the bowl. 2. Trace \textbf{\ar{ل}} once: tall upright, then the low curve. 3. Hide the models. Air-write the three teeth of \emph{sīn}, then the tall \emph{lām}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Point to:} \textbf{\ar{س}}, and say \emph{sīn}
  \item \emph{Point to:} \textbf{\ar{ل}}, and say \emph{lām}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{س} \ar{ل}} once, leaving them separate
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which way do Arabic words run? (\textbf{Right to left.}) Which letter has three teeth? (\textbf{\ar{س}, sīn.}) Which has the tall upright? (\textbf{\ar{ل}, lām.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alif, mīm — salām]{\ar{ا} and \ar{م} — finish \textbf{\ar{سلام}} without a cliff}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-alif-mim-salam}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ar{س}} and \textbf{\ar{ل}}. Add just two shapes, then the spoken word \emph{salām} becomes readable and writable.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — observe two new shapes}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ا}} is \emph{alif}: one clean upright carrying the long \emph{ā} here. From Phoenician \textbf{ʾālep} (\textquotedblleft{}ox\textquotedblright{}) — ancestor of Greek \emph{alpha} and Latin \textbf{A}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{م}} is \emph{mīm}: a small round head and a tail; it gives the final \emph{m}. From Phoenician \textbf{mem} (\textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{}) — sibling of Greek \emph{mu} and Latin \textbf{M}.
\end{itemize}

Arabic letters join — and a joined letter \textbf{changes shape}. The same letter looks different at the start, the middle and the end of a joined run. Its skeleton never changes (three teeth stay three teeth); only the connectors at its edges do. This is the one habit that makes Arabic read like handwriting rather than like print.

Watch all of it happen in one short word. In \textbf{\ar{سلام}}, \emph{sīn} reaches leftward into \emph{lām}; \emph{lām} and \emph{alif} fuse into the fixed pair \textbf{\ar{لا}}; then \emph{alif}, which never joins leftward, forces a pen lift before final \emph{mīm}.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, then delayed copy}
1. Point right to left: \textbf{\ar{س} · \ar{ل} · \ar{ا} · \ar{م}}. Say \emph{s · l · ā · m}. 2. Trace \textbf{\ar{سلام}} once: teeth, tall hook, upright, lift, round-headed \emph{mīm}. 3. Copy \textbf{\ar{سلام}} once while looking. 4. Cover it. Write it once from memory, then compare and correct one feature.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ar{سلام}}. (\textbf{salām, peace.}) What changes when a letter joins, and what stays the same? (\textbf{The connectors at its edges change; its skeleton does not.}) Where does the pen lift? (\textbf{After alif.}) Write the word once without looking. This is delayed recall, not penmanship perfection.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[marḥaban]{\emph{marḥaban} — make room for someone}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-marhaba}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{salām}. Now learn the light, everyday “hello” by ear before its written form asks anything of your eyes or hand.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Build three small beats: \emph{mar} — \emph{ḥa} — \emph{ban}. The middle consonant is a warm, breathy sound made deeper in the throat than English \emph{h}. Approximate it gently; clarity matters more than force.

\begin{quote}
\emph{marḥaban} = hello / welcome.
\end{quote}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
The root \textbf{r–ḥ–b} carries spaciousness: \emph{raḥb} is roomy. So \emph{marḥaban} is not an empty signal. It suggests, “There is room for you here.” A warm reply is \emph{marḥabtayn} — literally, “two welcomes.”
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mar} — \emph{ḥa} — \emph{ban}
  \item \emph{marḥaban}, keeping the middle consonant gentle
  \item \emph{marḥabtayn}, “two welcomes”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the root r–ḥ–b suggest? (\textbf{Room, spaciousness.}) Say the three beats of \emph{marḥaban}. The next two lessons reveal its new letter shapes in groups of two and three before you copy the whole greeting.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rāʾ, ḥāʾ]{\ar{ر} and \ar{ح} — two shapes inside \emph{marḥaban}}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-ra-ha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{marḥaban}. Its sound and welcome already belong to you. Now notice only two of its new written consonants.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — observe rāʾ and ḥāʾ}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ر}} is \emph{rāʾ}, the tapped \emph{r}. It curves down and left. It joins to what comes before it but not to what follows.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ح}} is \emph{ḥāʾ}, the deep, breathy \emph{ḥ}. Its open bowl has \textbf{no dot}.
\end{itemize}

Trace \textbf{\ar{ر} \ar{ح}} separately. Keep \emph{ḥāʾ} open and dotless.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rāʾ}, and trace \textbf{\ar{ر}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḥāʾ}, and trace \textbf{\ar{ح}}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{ر} \ar{ح}} once from memory, then compare
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter refuses to join forward? (\textbf{\ar{ر}.}) Which one is the dotless open bowl? (\textbf{\ar{ح}.}) Say \emph{marḥaban} again; the next step adds its final new skeleton and two dot-cousins.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bāʾ, tāʾ, thāʾ — marḥaban]{\ar{ب} \ar{ت} \ar{ث} — one bowl, three dot choices}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-ba-family-marhaba}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{\ar{ر}} and \textbf{\ar{ح}}. Today introduces one shared bowl and three dot patterns — exactly three new shapes — before you copy \emph{marḥaban}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one skeleton, three letters}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ب}} = \emph{bāʾ}: one dot \textbf{below}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ت}} = \emph{tāʾ}: two dots \textbf{above}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ث}} = \emph{thāʾ}: three dots \textbf{above}.
\end{itemize}

The dots are not decoration. They decide which letter you wrote. Trace the bowl once, then practise the three dot choices.

\textbf{\ar{ب}} comes from Phoenician \textbf{bēt} (\textquotedblleft{}house\textquotedblright{}) — ancestor of Greek \emph{beta} and Latin \textbf{B}. Put it beside the \emph{alif} you already know, from \textbf{ʾālep} (\textquotedblleft{}ox\textquotedblright{}), and you have the word \emph{alpha-bet}: the \textbf{ox} and the \textbf{house}, in that order, still naming every alphabet on earth.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, then delayed copy}
The greeting uses \textbf{\ar{ب}}. Its full form is \textbf{\ar{مرحبا}}.

1. Point right to left: \textbf{\ar{م} · \ar{ر} · \ar{ح} · \ar{ب} · \ar{ا}}. 2. Copy \textbf{\ar{مرحبا}} once while looking. 3. Cover it. Write it once from memory, then check the dot below \textbf{\ar{ب}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which cousin has one dot below? (\textbf{\ar{ب}.}) Two above? (\textbf{\ar{ت}.}) Three above? (\textbf{\ar{ث}.}) Read and write \textbf{\ar{مرحبا}} once: \emph{marḥaban}, “welcome.”
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{ال}]{\ar{ال} (al-) — \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} hiding in English \emph{algebra}}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-al}



\begin{quote}
Before the fuller greetings, one tiny, mighty word: Arabic's \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} You'll need it for \emph{the} peace, \emph{the} goodness — and you already know how to read it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} No new letters — just \textbf{\ar{ا}} (alif) and \textbf{\ar{ل}} (lām), the two you met in \emph{salām}, written together as \textbf{\ar{ال}} and \textbf{attached to the front} of a noun (Arabic glues \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} on; it isn't a separate word).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ال}} (\emph{al-}, \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}). For roughly 800 years Arabic was the Mediterranean's language of science and trade, and English and Spanish absorbed its words \textbf{with al- still attached}: \textbf{al}gebra (\emph{al-jabr}), \textbf{al}cohol (\emph{al-kuḥl}), \textbf{al}gorithm (\emph{al-Khwārizmī}), \textbf{al}chemy, \textbf{al}manac. Learning Arabic \emph{al-} is meeting an old friend you've been carrying in English all along.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: sun letters and moon letters}]
Here's a rule you can \emph{hear}. Before about half the consonants — the \textbf{sun letters} (\emph{s, sh, n, r, t, d}…) — the \emph{l} of \emph{al-} assimilates and the next letter \textbf{doubles}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{al-} + \emph{salām} $\to$ \textbf{as-salām} (not \textquotedblleft{}al-salām\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{al-} + \emph{nūr} $\to$ \textbf{an-nūr}
\end{itemize}

Before the \textbf{moon letters} (\emph{kh, k, b, m}…) the \emph{l} stays clear: \textbf{al-khayr}, \textbf{al-bab}. You can still hear this rule fossilized in Spanish \emph{azúcar}, from Arabic \emph{as-sukkar} (\textquotedblleft{}the sugar\textquotedblright{}) — the \emph{l} long gone, the doubled \emph{s} remaining.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}al-\textquotedblright{} and three English words hiding it — al-gebra, al-cohol, al-manac
  \item sun-letter assimilation — al- + salām $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}as-salām\textquotedblright{}
  \item moon-letter, no change — al- + khayr $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}al-khayr\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{ال}} mean, and how does it attach? (\textquotedblleft{}The,\textquotedblright{} glued to the front of its noun.) What happens before a \emph{sun letter} like \emph{s}? (The \emph{l} assimilates and the letter doubles — \emph{as-salām}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[as-salāmu ʿalaykum]{\emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} — offer the full greeting by ear}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-as-salamu-alaykum}



\begin{quote}
You already own \emph{salām} and \emph{al-}. Now speak the full greeting before decoding or copying its unfamiliar second half.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say \emph{as-salāmu} — then \emph{ʿalaykum}. In \emph{ʿalaykum}, begin with a light tightening deep in the throat. That sound is \emph{ʿayn}; an approximation is enough today.

\begin{quote}
\emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} = peace be upon you.
\end{quote}

The \emph{l} of \emph{al-} blends into the following \emph{s}, so \emph{al-salām} is pronounced \emph{as-salām}. Arabic then places “the peace” beside “upon you” and leaves the verb “is” understood.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{The exchange — the reply}
The fixed reply is \emph{wa-ʿalaykum as-salām}: “and upon you, peace.” Hear the little \emph{wa-} at the front; it means “and.”

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{as-salāmu} — \emph{ʿalaykum}
  \item the complete greeting once, slowly
  \item \emph{wa-ʿalaykum as-salām}, the reply
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two spoken blocks? (\textbf{as-salāmu + ʿalaykum.}) Where is the word “is”? (\textbf{It is understood.}) Speak the greeting and reply once. The next two lessons reveal the remaining shapes before showing the full line.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ʿayn, yāʾ]{\ar{ع} and \ar{ي} — open \emph{ʿalaykum} gently}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-ayn-ya}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum}. Only after speaking the whole greeting do you meet two shapes from its second block.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — observe ʿayn and yāʾ}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ع}} is \emph{ʿayn}, the deep opening sound in \emph{ʿalaykum}. Notice its curved hook.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ي}} is \emph{yāʾ}, the \emph{y} sound. In isolation it carries two dots below.
\end{itemize}

Trace each once. Then point right to left at \textbf{\ar{ع} \ar{ي}} while saying \emph{ʿ — y}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\ar{ع}}, and say \emph{ʿayn}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\ar{ي}}, and say \emph{yāʾ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} both once from memory, then compare
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape begins the throat sound? (\textbf{\ar{ع}.}) Which has two dots below when isolated? (\textbf{\ar{ي}.}) No whole phrase yet; two final shapes come next.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāf, wāw — as-salāmu ʿalaykum]{\ar{ك} and \ar{و} — complete the greeting after the sound}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-kaf-waw-alaykum}



\begin{quote}
You can speak the greeting and recognize \textbf{\ar{ع}} and \textbf{\ar{ي}}. Add just two shapes, then copy the complete line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — observe two new shapes}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ك}} is \emph{kāf}, the \emph{k} near the end of \emph{ʿalaykum}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{و}} is \emph{wāw}, the \emph{w} in the reply’s opening \emph{wa-}, “and.” Like \textbf{\ar{ر}}, it does not join to the letter after it.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, then delayed copy}
1. Find the familiar peace word inside \textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}}. 2. Point through the second block, \textbf{\ar{عليكم}}, right to left. 3. Copy \textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}} once while looking. 4. Cover it. Write \textbf{\ar{عليكم}} from memory, then compare and correct one shape. 5. Add \textbf{\ar{و}} before that block to begin the reply: \textbf{\ar{وعليكم}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter gives the \emph{k}? (\textbf{\ar{ك}.}) Which gives \emph{wa-}, “and”? (\textbf{\ar{و}.}) Read \textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}}, then write the shorter block \textbf{\ar{عليكم}} without looking.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[as-salāmu ʿalaykum]{\emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} — hear, write, repair}

\label{lesson:AR-W00-full-greeting-recall}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} once. Then turn the page or cover every Arabic model. This lesson adds no shape and no new phrase.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — dictation and repair}
1. Hear or read the romanization \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum}. 2. Write the Arabic greeting from memory. 3. Reveal \textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}}. 4. Compare from right to left. Circle one uncertain shape and repair it once.

Stop after one repaired attempt. Retrieval is the goal; repetition without attention is not.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}} aloud. Which part did you repair? Cover the model and write only \textbf{\ar{عليكم}} once more if that repair still feels uncertain.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير}]{\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير} (ṣabāḥ al-khayr) — \textquotedblleft{}morning of goodness\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-sabah-al-khayr}



\begin{quote}
Time-of-day greetings — built, like everything, from roots and the attached \emph{al-}. And a chance to hear two sounds English doesn't have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} Two new letters:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ص}} = \emph{ṣād}, an \textbf{emphatic} (heavy, dark) \textquotedblleft{}s\textquotedblright{} — a \emph{different} letter from the light \textbf{\ar{س}} you know.
  \item \textbf{\ar{خ}} = \emph{khāʾ}, a throat-scrape from the back of the mouth — the \textbf{same sound as Spanish \emph{j}} (as in \emph{José}), or the \emph{ch} in Scottish \emph{loch}.
\end{itemize}

With the rest known, read \textbf{\ar{صباح}} (\emph{ṣabāḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\ar{خير}} (\emph{khayr}, \textquotedblleft{}goodness\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{صباح}} (\emph{ṣabāḥ}), root \textbf{ṣ–b–ḥ} (dawn/waking: \emph{ṣubḥ} \textquotedblleft{}dawn,\textquotedblright{} \emph{aṣbaḥa} \textquotedblleft{}to become / reach morning\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{\ar{خير}} (\emph{khayr}, \textquotedblleft{}good, goodness\textquotedblright{}), root \textbf{kh–y–r}. Together \textbf{\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير}} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning of the goodness}.\textquotedblright{} Note \emph{al-khayr} keeps its \emph{l} — \textbf{\ar{خ}} is a \emph{moon letter} — a clean contrast with \emph{as-salām}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The reply mirrors it beautifully: \textbf{\ar{صباح} \ar{النور}} (\emph{ṣabāḥ an-nūr}) — \textquotedblleft{}morning of the \textbf{light}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{al-} + \emph{nūr}, sun-letter \emph{n} assimilated). You wish someone goodness; they wish you light back.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ṣabāḥ al-khayr\textquotedblright{} — the heavy ṣ, then the throat-scrape kh
  \item why \emph{al-khayr} keeps its \emph{l} (\ar{خ} is a moon letter)
  \item the reply — \textquotedblleft{}ṣabāḥ an-nūr\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}morning of light\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير}}. What are the two roots? (\emph{ṣ–b–ḥ} \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} \emph{kh–y–r} \textquotedblleft{}goodness.\textquotedblright{}) Why is it \emph{al-khayr} but \emph{as-salām}? (\ar{خ} is a moon letter — \emph{l} stays; \emph{s} is a sun letter — \emph{l} assimilates.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{مساء} \ar{الخير}]{\ar{مساء} \ar{الخير} (masāʾ al-khayr) — \textquotedblleft{}evening of goodness\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-masa-al-khayr}



\begin{quote}
The evening twin of \emph{ṣabāḥ al-khayr} — and Arabic's tidy habit of naming morning and evening as matched events.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} One new mark:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ء}} = \emph{hamza}, a \textbf{glottal stop} — the little catch in the middle of \textquotedblleft{}uh-oh.\textquotedblright{} At the end of \textbf{\ar{مساء}} it closes the word: \emph{masāʾ}.
\end{itemize}

Everything else — \textbf{\ar{م} \ar{س} \ar{ا}} and the \textbf{\ar{الخير}} you read last lesson — is already yours.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{مساء}} (\emph{masāʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{}), root \textbf{m–s–w}: \emph{amsā}, \textquotedblleft{}to become / reach evening\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{exact mirror} of \emph{aṣbaḥa} (\textquotedblleft{}to reach morning\textquotedblright{}). Arabic names the two ends of the day as matched events, each with its own \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{} verb, where French \emph{soir} and Spanish \emph{tarde} both merely meant \textquotedblleft{}late.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\ar{مساء} \ar{الخير}} = \textquotedblleft{}evening of goodness\textquotedblright{}; reply \textbf{\ar{مساء} \ar{النور}} (\emph{masāʾ an-nūr}), \textquotedblleft{}evening of light.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The symmetry is the point: morning and evening are greeted with the \emph{same} structure (\textquotedblleft{}{[}time{]} of goodness\textquotedblright{}) and answered with the \emph{same} structure (\textquotedblleft{}{[}time{]} of light\textquotedblright{}). Learn one pair, you have both.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}masāʾ al-khayr\textquotedblright{} — the glottal catch at the end of \emph{masāʾ}
  \item the mirror — \emph{aṣbaḥa} (reach morning) / \emph{amsā} (reach evening)
  \item the reply — \textquotedblleft{}masāʾ an-nūr\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ar{مساء} \ar{الخير}}. What does the mark \textbf{\ar{ء}} (hamza) do? (A glottal stop — the catch in \textquotedblleft{}uh-oh.\textquotedblright{}) How does Arabic treat morning and evening differently from French/Spanish? (As matched \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{} events, not just \textquotedblleft{}late.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{شكرا}]{\ar{شكرا} (shukran) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-shukran}



\begin{quote}
The word for gratitude — and a chance to watch the root-and-pattern engine do its trick on a brand-new root.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} Two new letters:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ش}} = \emph{shīn}, \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{} — it is simply \textbf{\ar{س}} (\emph{sīn}) \textbf{plus three dots} on top (the dots-on-a-skeleton idea again).
  \item \textbf{\ar{ك}} = \emph{kāf}, \textquotedblleft{}k\textquotedblright{} — already met inside \emph{ʿalaykum}.
\end{itemize}

Read \textbf{\ar{شكرا}} right to left $\to$ \emph{shukran}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{شكرا}} (\emph{shukran}), root \textbf{sh–k–r} (\emph{gratitude}): \emph{shukr} (\textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}), \emph{shākir} (\textquotedblleft{}thankful\textquotedblright{}), \emph{mashkūr} (\textquotedblleft{}thanked\textquotedblright{}). Look closely: \emph{shākir} and \emph{mashkūr} sit in the \textbf{exact same patterns} as \emph{kātib} (\textquotedblleft{}writer\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{maktūb} (\textquotedblleft{}written\textquotedblright{}) from the root engine — \emph{fāʿil} (the doer) and \emph{mafʿūl} (the done-to). Learn a pattern once and it works on every root.

And it travels: this same Semitic root \textbf{sh–k–r}, carried through Persian, is the source of Hindi/Urdu \emph{shukriyā} (\textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The reply is gentle: \textbf{\ar{عفوا}} (\emph{ʿafwan}), \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing / you're pardoned\textquotedblright{} — from a root meaning to forgive or waive. You thank; they wave it away.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read right to left — shuk · ran $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}shukran\textquotedblright{}
  \item how \ar{ش} is just \ar{س} with three dots
  \item the pattern echo — \emph{shākir/mashkūr} like \emph{kātib/maktūb}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ar{شكرا}}. What is its root, and what two familiar patterns do \emph{shākir} and \emph{mashkūr} follow? (\emph{sh–k–r}; the \emph{kātib} / \emph{maktūb} patterns — doer and done-to.) The reply to \emph{shukran}? (\emph{ʿafwan}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — the day of greetings}

\label{lesson:AR-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
A dozen letters, learned one greeting at a time, and now the whole day of Arabic greetings and their fixed replies.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Read them back}
Sound each out \textbf{right to left} before checking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Read} & \textbf{} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{سلام}} & \emph{salām} & peace \\
\textbf{\ar{مرحبا}} & \emph{marḥaban} & welcome / hi \\
\textbf{\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}} & \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} & peace be upon you \\
\textbf{\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير}} & \emph{ṣabāḥ al-khayr} & good morning \\
\textbf{\ar{مساء} \ar{الخير}} & \emph{masāʾ al-khayr} & good evening \\
\textbf{\ar{شكرا}} & \emph{shukran} & thank you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The exchange — greetings and replies}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{When} & \textbf{Greeting} & \textbf{Reply} \\
\midrule
casual & \emph{marḥaban} & \emph{marḥabtayn} (\textquotedblleft{}two welcomes\textquotedblright{}) \\
any time & \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} & \emph{wa-ʿalaykum as-salām} \\
morning & \emph{ṣabāḥ al-khayr} & \emph{ṣabāḥ an-nūr} (\textquotedblleft{}morning of light\textquotedblright{}) \\
evening & \emph{masāʾ al-khayr} & \emph{masāʾ an-nūr} \\
thanks & \emph{shukran} & \emph{ʿafwan} (\textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two engines did all of it: the three-consonant \textbf{root} (\emph{s-l-m}, \emph{sh-k-r}, \emph{ṣ-b-ḥ}…) and the attached \textbf{al-} with its sun/moon assimilation (\emph{as-salām} but \emph{al-khayr}). The letters arrived inside real words — about a dozen of them, half the alphabet — never as a chart to memorize.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all six greetings, right to left
  \item \emph{Say it:} each greeting with its reply — \textquotedblleft{}as-salāmu ʿalaykum\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}wa-ʿalaykum as-salām\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} greet, then thank — \textquotedblleft{}ṣabāḥ al-khayr!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}shukran.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Write it:} hear \emph{salām}, write \textbf{\ar{سلام}} without looking, then compare and repair one shape
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read all six greetings aloud, right to left. Name the two \textquotedblleft{}engines\textquotedblright{} that build them. (The three-consonant \emph{root}, and the attached \emph{al-} with sun/moon assimilation.)

Next chapter: introducing yourself — \emph{ismī…} (\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}) — and how Arabic marks \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} by \textbf{gender} (\emph{anta} to a man, \emph{anti} to a woman), a different axis from the formal/informal split of the European languages.
\end{tcolorbox}
